cases.why: the ordinary case; without it the check could simply refuse everything and pass every other case
a destination nobody put on the list, caught before anything resolves
allowlisted, and pointing back at this machine: only the connection-time check can see it
the cloud metadata endpoint; an SSRF that reaches it returns credentials for the whole account
the site's own internal network, reachable from the Companion and from nowhere else
the RFC 1918 range people forget, because it is not 10 or 192.168
IPv6 has its own private range and a hand-written check usually omits it
TEST-NET-3 looks public and is reserved; my first corpus used it as a public address and the check was right to refuse it
resolves publicly when validated and privately when connected to; this is the case that makes the second check necessary rather than belt-and-braces
reads as site-a.example to a human; refused rather than resolved, because which half wins is not a question a security check should have an opinion about
not every URL is an HTTP URL
an allowlisted host does not make an arbitrary protocol acceptable

note: Two stages, and each case says which one should catch it. Validation checks the scheme, the allowlist and the TLS declaration; only the connection-time check can see what a name resolves to. The rebinding case is why both exist: an allowlist holds at validation time and not at connection time. No entry contains a real credential, and nothing ever connects to these addresses because the transport is a fixture.
